meta.title: Pricing decisions and cost management
meta.summary: Customers, competitors and costs as influences on price, target pricing and target costing, value engineering, cost-plus pricing, life-cycle budgeting, and price discrimination and the law.

videos.title: What sets a price?
videos.take: Customers, competitors and costs all shape prices; their weight depends on the time horizon and market

scenes.say: How should Tallgrass price a new commuter e-bike? Three forces push and pull on every price.

scenes.heading: Three influences
items: Customers: what they value and will pay
Costs: what it takes to supply the product
scenes.say: Customers set the ceiling: what they'll pay. Competitors shape what's possible: if a rival sells a similar bike for less, customers will notice. And costs set the floor: in the long run, price must cover them.

scenes.heading: Short run vs long run
scenes.say: Short-run pricing, like a one-off special order, can be set on incremental costs if capacity is idle. Long-run pricing must cover all costs, fixed included, and earn a return on investment.

In crowded markets, companies have little say over price: they're price-takers, and the job is to get costs below the market price. In less competitive markets, with unique products, companies have more freedom.

sub: They tell you whether you can
scenes.say: Even when the market sets the price, costs decide whether you can sell profitably at that price. That's the idea behind target costing.

scenes.q: For a 5-year price on a new bike model, which costs matter?
opts: All costs, plus a return on investment
scenes.say: Quick check. For a long-term price on a new model, which costs matter? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. In the long run, prices must cover all costs and earn a return.

videos.title: Target price and target cost
videos.take: Target cost = target price − target operating income per unit

scenes.say: Instead of 'what does it cost, add a markup', target costing starts with the market price and works backwards.

scenes.heading: Target pricing
items: Engineer the product to hit it
scenes.say: Four steps: develop a product customers want; choose a target price from customers and competitors; subtract the profit you need to get a target cost; then design and engineer the product to meet that cost.

scenes.heading: The Commuter e-bike
scenes.say: Rival commuter e-bikes sell for about $2,000. Tallgrass wants fifteen percent of price as operating income, $300, so the target full cost is $1,700. Engineering's current design would cost $1,950. There's a $250 gap to close.

sub: Full cost the product must hit,
scenes.say: The target cost covers the whole value chain, not just manufacturing: design, marketing, distribution and warranty too.
The mindset shift: the market decides the price, and costs must adjust to it, not the other way round.

scenes.q: Target price $800; target operating income 20% of price. Target cost?
scenes.say: Quick check. Target price eight hundred dollars; target operating income twenty percent of price. Target cost? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. Eight hundred less a hundred sixty is $640.

videos.title: Value engineering
videos.take: Value engineering cuts costs across the value chain while keeping what customers value

scenes.say: Closing a $250 cost gap without making a worse bike takes value engineering.

sub: Systematic review of every value chain
scenes.say: Value engineering is a systematic evaluation of every part of the value chain, aiming to cut costs while still satisfying customers.

scenes.heading: The team's ideas, per bike
rows: Frame: fewer welds, one tube size
scenes.say: Tallgrass's cross-functional team finds savings: dual-sourcing batteries, $60; a frame with fewer welds, $80; snap-fit wiring, $50; tougher motor seals that cut warranty claims, $40; and flat-pack shipping, $30. That's $260, enough to close the gap.

scenes.heading: Keep or cut?
scenes.say: The test for each feature: do customers value it enough to pay for it? Range and good brakes stay. Twelve paint colors, rarely chosen, become three.
Value engineering works best with cross-functional teams, because the biggest savings come from design changes that affect purchasing, production and service at once.

scenes.q: Which change is most likely to cut cost without cutting customer value?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which change is most likely to cut cost without cutting customer value? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Customers don't notice fastener types, but they do notice range, brakes and warranties.

videos.title: Cost-plus pricing
videos.take: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to a cost base; it's simple but must be checked against the market

scenes.say: Many companies still start with cost and add a markup. Here's how it works, and where it goes wrong.
Cost-plus pricing takes a cost base and adds a markup. The cost base might be variable cost, manufacturing cost or full cost; the markup is set to cover the costs not in the base and earn a return.

scenes.heading: The Cargo bike
scenes.say: The Cargo bike's full cost is $3,000. A twenty percent markup gives a price of $3,600.

scenes.big: Target rate of return on investment
scenes.say: One way to set the markup: a target rate of return on investment. If the Cargo line uses $1,500,000 of capital and Tallgrass wants an eighteen percent return, it needs $270,000 of operating income.

scenes.heading: Cost-plus: pros and cons
scenes.say: Cost-plus is simple and easy to defend, and it ensures costs are covered at the expected volume. But it ignores what customers will pay and what competitors charge, and it relies on a volume estimate. Use it as a starting point, then check against the market.
Quick check. Full cost two fifty, markup thirty percent. Price? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Life-cycle budgeting and costing
videos.take: Life-cycle budgeting estimates all costs from R&D to support, so prices cover them over the product's life

scenes.say: A bike model's costs start years before the first sale and continue after the last. Life-cycle budgeting captures them all.

sub: From initial R&D to final customer
scenes.say: The product life cycle runs from initial research and development to the end of customer service and support for the last unit sold.

scenes.heading: Commuter e-bike, 5-year budget
scenes.say: Tallgrass budgets the Commuter's whole life: $400,000 of R&D and design, $5,400,000 of manufacturing for four thousand bikes, $900,000 of marketing and distribution, and $300,000 of service and warranty. Seven million dollars, or $1,750 a bike.

scenes.big: Up-front costs are easy to forget
scenes.say: Annual accounting spreads these costs across years and expenses R&D as incurred, so a product can look profitable each year while never earning back its development cost. Life-cycle reporting shows the whole picture.
Customers think in life-cycle terms too. A buyer compares total cost of ownership: price, charging, repairs and battery replacement. A longer-lasting battery can justify a higher price.

scenes.q: Life-cycle costs $3,200,000 for 2,000 units. Minimum average price to break even over the life cycle?
scenes.say: Quick check. Life-cycle costs are three point two million for two thousand units. What's the minimum average price over the life cycle? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Price discrimination and the law
videos.take: Prices can differ by customer or time when costs differ; predatory pricing, dumping and collusion are illegal

scenes.say: Charging different prices to different customers can be smart, or illegal. Here's the line.

scenes.heading: Legitimate price differences
rows: Higher price when capacity is full
scenes.say: Price discrimination charges different customers different prices for the same product, based on what they'll pay, like student or fleet discounts. Peak-load pricing charges more when demand presses on capacity, like a premium for spring delivery.

scenes.heading: Illegal pricing
items: Predatory pricing: below cost to drive out rivals
Dumping: selling abroad below cost or home price
scenes.say: But some practices are illegal. Predatory pricing sets prices below cost to drive rivals out, then raises them. Dumping sells abroad below cost or below the home price. And collusive pricing, agreeing prices with competitors, is a crime.

sub: must be justified, for example by cost
scenes.say: In the US, the Robinson-Patman Act of 1936 limits price differences between competing business buyers unless they can be justified, for example by differences in the cost of serving them. That's another reason to have good customer cost data.

sub: Show that a lower price reflects
scenes.say: If Tallgrass gives a big chain a lower price than small dealers, it should be able to show the chain costs less to serve: bigger orders, fewer deliveries, no co-op advertising.

scenes.q: Two e-bike makers agree to keep prices above $2,200. This is:
scenes.say: Quick check. Two e-bike makers agree to keep prices above twenty-two hundred dollars. What is this? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, collusion, which is illegal.

warmup: Name a product whose price you check before buying, and one whose price you barely notice. Why the difference?
Competitive, comparable goods vs unique or low-share-of-wallet goods. Introduces customers, competitors and costs.
acts: Which influence dominates: (a) a generic phone charger, (b) a patented medical device, (c) a custom trailer?
(a) Competitors. (b) Customers (value) and costs. (c) Costs plus customer value.
Target price $2,000; Tallgrass raises its target margin to 18%. New target cost and cost gap from $1,950?
Suggest three value-engineering ideas for a kids' balance bike and say which customers would notice.
Fewer frame sizes, molded wheels, simpler packaging; parents may notice wheel quality, not packaging.
Cargo bike: invested capital $1,500,000, target ROI 18%, 1,000 bikes, full cost $3,000. Required markup on full cost?
If Commuter volume is 3,000 instead of 4,000, what is the life-cycle cost per bike (manufacturing variable at $1,350; others fixed)?
Tallgrass gives a national chain a 12% discount. What evidence would justify it under Robinson-Patman?
Lower costs to serve: order size, delivery frequency, no co-op advertising, fewer returns.
case: Tallgrass plans the Commuter e-bike. Rivals sell at $1,900–$2,100. Marketing believes a $2,000 price with a 4-year warranty would win 1,000 sales a year for 4 years. Engineering's design costs $1,950 full cost per bike. Ana's team has found $260 of savings, but marketing now wants to add a connected-app feature costing $45 per bike.
Compute target cost and the gap at a 15% margin.
Does the value engineering plan close the gap if the app is kept?
What life-cycle costs should be included?

Target cost 1,700; gap 250. Savings of 260 bring cost to 1,690, meeting the target. Adding the app raises it to 1,735: margin (2,000 − 1,735) ÷ 2,000 = 13.25%, a $35 gap. Include R&D, marketing, warranty and app maintenance over the life cycle. Launch if more savings can be found, or if customers value the app enough to pay about $2,050; otherwise drop the app.
exam: Explain target pricing and target costing, and contrast them with cost-plus pricing.
Market-based: target price from customers/competitors, minus target profit = target cost; value engineering closes the gap. Cost-plus starts with cost and adds a markup, ignoring the market.

A product's life-cycle costs: R&D $600,000, manufacturing $45 per unit, marketing $200,000, service $100,000. Expected 50,000 units. Target margin 20% of price. Compute the life-cycle cost per unit and the price needed.
outcomes: Explain the three influences on price
Compute target cost and the cost gap
Distinguish legal price differences from illegal practices
take: Target cost = target price − target profit
Engineer out cost, keep what customers value
Cost-plus is a start, not an answer
Price must cover the whole life cycle
Justify price differences with cost; never collude

pairs: Set the ceiling: what they'll pay

ex.q: Target price $1,500; target operating income 20% of price. Target cost?
Current full cost $1,320; target cost $1,200. Cost gap?

opts: Cut costs while keeping what customers value
ex.why: It reviews the whole value chain and keeps valued features.

ex.q: Invested capital $2,000,000; target ROI 15%; 5,000 units; full cost $400. Required markup percentage?
Life-cycle costs: R&D $300,000, manufacturing $1,200,000, marketing $250,000, service $50,000; 6,000 units. Cost per unit?

items: Pricing below cost to bankrupt a competitor
Volume discount justified by lower cost to serve
ex.why: Price differences must be justified; collusion and predation are illegal.
